doc.title: Joanne Brackeen interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 10, 2001

title: How she got the Art Blakey job at Slug's
summary: Living near Slug's with four children, she sat in with Blakey's band and was hired at the end of the set.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah, I guess it does. How did the gig with Blakey come about?
Oh, that’s an interesting story. I lived right around the corner from this club called Slug’s.
Oh, Slug’s, I’ve heard this name, yes.

A tiny club. I mean it was bigger than this room, but not that much. It had sawdust all over the floor and you could get a beer for a dollar, and all the major groups were there. Art Blakey, Freddie Hubbard, McCoy Tyner, everybody, Lee Morgan. Everybody worked in there. And I lived right around the corner. So but I lived up like six flights of stairs, and I had four kids in five years, and they were very young, so I didn’t get out too often. So one night I heard that Art Blakey was there and I though oh I’ve got enough energy, I’m going to go around and see the band. So I’m saying this because I was kind of spaced out. It was late at night, and I also got up early in the morning. So I walked in there, and here was Art’s band. And they just sounded incredible. It was amazing music. And the piano player was sitting up there but he wasn’t playing. And it sounded like he should have been playing, it sounded like they needed the piano to play, you know, with the energy that they were playing in right there. So because I’m so spaced out, I’m just only hearing the music, I walked up to the bandstand and say, “Do you mind if I play?” And the piano player said, “No, go ahead.” It sounds funny but if you ever have four kids and you’re going six flights of stairs up and down for everything you’re doing during the whole day, by the time you get to the music it’s just, you’re so happy that you forget. And that’s what happened. And at the end of the set he looked up and saw me and I was hired. It was the furthest thing from my mind.
